question: A 2-year-old presents with 3 days of fever and cough. Examination reveals tachypnoea, subcostal retractions, and decreased breath sounds on the right. She is feeding poorly. Which imaging decision best applies ALARA principles?

answers.text: Order a CXR immediately; imaging is always required to confirm pneumonia before starting antibiotics

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Routine CXR is NOT indicated for uncomplicated clinical pneumonia. Clinical diagnosis alone guides antibiotic choice in a well child.

answers.text: Order a CXR now, as this child has signs suggesting complicated pneumonia (poor feeding, decreased breath sounds)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Signs of possible complications — decreased air entry, feeding difficulty — are indications for CXR. ALARA means imaging when it will change management, not never imaging.

answers.text: Order a CT chest immediately to exclude parapneumonic effusion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: CT is not the first-line investigation. CXR ± ultrasound can detect effusion with far lower radiation dose.

answers.text: Withhold all imaging and reassess in 48 hours regardless of clinical features

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Watchful waiting is appropriate for mild uncomplicated illness, but this child's signs of decreased air entry and poor feeding warrant imaging now.

overallFeedback.feedback: Recall ALARA: radiation exposure must be justified. For uncomplicated clinical pneumonia, no imaging is needed; for signs of complication, CXR is indicated and appropriate.
Well done. ALARA is not 'never image' — it is 'image only when the result will change management'. Signs of complication justify CXR.
